name: Carlos Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run the tin seamer at a soup plant. My vocational certificate taught me how to measure a folded seam, and I still cut open test cans every shift. I like the click when the line settles into rhythm; scraping a jam of crushed tins beside a hot motor is the part I dread.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cleans offices in the mornings. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. My pay is low for an experienced operator and there are few similar jobs nearby. I never use AI tools; I check the gauge and ask the maintenance crew when the seamer sounds wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my shift that a computer can shuffle the can orders, but a tin with a loose seam will still leak. We will keep listening to the seamer and pulling test cans. I don't see a reason to celebrate a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The canning plant pays below what an experienced operator ought to earn, and we have only three weeks of bills saved. My partner cleans offices in the morning, but with two school-age children and a mortgage, a broken car is a serious problem. There are few other canning jobs near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the tin seamer and cutting open a test can each shift to measure its fold. I never use AI and I won't start for an order sheet that changes nothing on the floor. I'll take the next Saturday shift offered to put new wages toward our car repair bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary bills, even if the technology stops making headlines. The seam has to hold while the bank payment still goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you know a seam is good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cut a test tin open with the seam saw, then measure the folded metal with a gauge from my vocational course. A clicking seamer tells me something is wrong before the screen does. The can has to hold soup all the way to a family's cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last surprise bill do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the car needed a new tyre; we paid the mortgage and delayed buying school coats until the next wage. One more bill like that would leave nothing in the account. Saturday pay would fill that hole, if the plant actually offers the shift.

say: A **loose tin seam** can leak despite a tidier computer order sheet.
Our shift still needs **test cans** and an operator listening to the seamer.
think: Three weeks of **savings** cannot cover many surprise bills.
Our **low factory pay** and few local canning jobs keep the mortgage worrying.
do: **Keep** setting the tin seamer and measuring cut-open test cans.
**Take** an offered Saturday shift and use new wages on the car repair bill.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills with a thin cushion.
S0.quote: The can has to hold soup all the way to a family's cupboard.
fieldNote: Carlos **never uses AI** and relies on sound, gauges and his vocational instruction at the seamer.
His **Saturday pay plan** depends on an offered shift and addresses a real car bill beside the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep setting tin seamer and gauging cut-open test cans
Take offered Saturday shift to pay car repair bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may let AI write schedules and buy tin before robots can work the line. Somebody will still need to check whether each seamer is sealing. If management changes the shift sheet, they should say which paid hours remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am average at the job, not the special technician. My partner's cleaning hours are fixed, and our savings would not cover even a month if my shift were shortened. I worry the new scheduling software could make the whole plant squeeze the night crew before any robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the shift supervisor for the posted roster and compare it with my last three pay slips. I'll keep checking seams on the current machine. If the plant requires a real paid course on its new line controls, I'll attend with a trainer on a stopped seamer; I won't pay for a screen course myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A changed roster can take money out of our kitchen before anyone buys a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does one lost shift mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three paid night shifts a week is what keeps the mortgage and food covered. A new schedule with two shifts would leave a hole my partner's cleaning wage cannot fill. I need the actual roster, not a rumour at the time clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer would have to show me how to isolate the motor and test a bad seam without reaching across moving tins. If the paid course is required and offered, I will learn it. Watching a demonstration at lunch is not enough for me.

say: **AI scheduling** may change paid hours before robots touch the canning line.
Management should post the **roster** and say who still checks tin seams.
think: My **average standing** gives no guarantee if the night crew shrinks.
Less than a month of **savings** cannot replace a lost weekly shift.
do: **Compare** the posted roster with three actual pay slips.
**Keep** gauging seamer tests on the current line.
**Attend** required paid line-control training if an offered trainer-led place is safe.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic reduction in night-shift income.
S1.quote: A changed roster can take money out of our kitchen before anyone buys a robot.
fieldNote: He will **check a real roster** before assuming hours are lost, while the thin reserve makes the possibility immediate.
His **training condition** is a required paid place with a trainer and stopped machine, not casual observation.

steps.text: Compare posted night roster with last three pay slips
Keep gauging can seams on current line
Attend line-control course if required paid safe trainer-led place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family that thinking AI in 2028 might take over can orders, then capable robots around 2031 might run and check the seamers. I don't want anyone telling us a computer will somehow pay the mortgage. We need a written plan from the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the robots can do the hands-on work. I think the plant would drop most seamer shifts, including mine, and three weeks saved would be gone at once. My partner's cleaning wage could not carry the children and mortgage. I have been lying awake over much smaller bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the supervisor for written notice and any real paid work left after robot installation. We'll cancel the sports subscription and stop eating takeaway to keep the mortgage current. If my hours are cut, I'll apply to posted local warehouse or food-packing jobs only where the safe duties, regular base pay and school pickup times work; I'll ask my older sister about temporary child pickup if an offered shift is awkward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can work a hard shift; I can't make another soup plant appear near our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first money to go would be the sports subscription and the Friday takeaway. Neither saves a whole wage, but it keeps the mortgage payment from sliding while I make applications. I wouldn't tell the children the house is safe until I know the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your sister cover a new shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older sister lives near the school and could sometimes collect the children, but I would ask first. I cannot put her down as permanent child care on an application. The posted job still needs regular pay, not just an overtime promise.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes orders before capable robots reach seamers around 2031.
The plant owes workers a **written work plan**, not a vague promise about mortgages.
think: At **48**, I expect most seamer hours could vanish.
Our **three-week reserve** and one cleaning wage cannot carry children and mortgage.
do: **Ask** supervisor for written notice and remaining paid work.
**Cancel** sports subscription and takeaway to protect mortgage payments.
**Apply** to posted safe local packing work if hours cut, base pay and pickup fit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major lost hours and existing sleepless bill worries.
S2.quote: I can work a hard shift; I can't make another soup plant appear near our home.
fieldNote: He expects **major shift loss** by 2031 and connects it to current sleepless money pressure.
His **job applications** require actual local postings, safe duties, base pay and workable pickup; sisterly help is requested, not assumed.

steps.text: Ask supervisor for written robot notice and remaining paid work
Cancel sports subscription and Friday takeaway for mortgage
Apply to posted safe local packing jobs if hours cut, base pay and pickup fit
Ask older sister about occasional school pickup if offered shift conflicts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI might change can orders in 2031, but the capable robots would not work our seamer line until around 2034. Five years is time to read the wage slips and make a sensible plan. I am not signing up for every new gadget on a noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots can handle the tins. We still have a mortgage and the children would be older, but I can't assume the loan is gone. If full shifts continue, the Saturday pay could build a reserve; if the line cuts hours early, the plan gets smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for one extra paid Saturday a month and save that new wage after the tyre bill is cleared. I'll check the plant's actual staffing notices every quarter. If they offer a funded paid practical course to inspect robot-made seams, with a trainer and guarded machine, I'll attend; after qualifying, if seamer shifts are cut, I'll apply to posted local quality jobs with safe duties and enough base pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can count five years. Counting is easier than guessing what a shiny arm does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical inspection teaching involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course must include opening a badly folded tin and measuring the seam, then stopping the line when the gauge is wrong. I would need paid time and the fees covered. We cannot spend the children's school money on an optional certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply for quality work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply only after I have the qualification and the shift actually loses hours. A posted quality job has to pay enough without relying on weekend overtime, and the trip must let one of us collect the children. A title alone means nothing.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes orders before capable robots reach seamers around 2034.
Five years gives workers time to **check wages** and real staffing plans.
think: At **51**, the mortgage may still depend on seamer wages.
Extra paid **Saturday shifts** could build savings only if the plant offers them.
do: **Save** new paid Saturday wages after the tyre bill.
**Attend** funded paid guarded seam-inspection training if offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local quality jobs only if qualified, hours fall, base pay covers bills and travel allows school pickup.
feel: **Anxious** about future paid hours but able to plan by actual notices.
S3.quote: A posted quality job has to pay enough without relying on weekend overtime, and the trip must let one of us collect the children.
fieldNote: His **new saving** depends on an offered extra paid shift and follows a specific tyre bill.
The **quality application** follows qualification and actual hour cuts; title or hypothetical openings do not count as employment.

steps.text: Save wages from offered extra Saturday shift after tyre bill
Check actual plant staffing notices each quarter
Attend seam-inspection course if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply if qualified after cuts to posted safe local quality work with bill-covering pay, school-compatible travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan tin orders by 2036, then capable robots might handle the seamers around 2039. Ten years leaves more room to pay down the mortgage. I would tell the shift to ask about actual jobs before arguing over a machine that has not been ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when the physical robots arrive. The children may be grown, but I don't know what their costs or our mortgage balance will be. Low factory pay still leaves us under a month ahead today. I can use a decade, but I can't spend it pretending the bills wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the seamer job and, when an extra paid shift comes through, pay that new money straight off the mortgage after current bills. I'll ask the supervisor twice a year whether the plant has ordered robot seamers and what paid roles are posted. If the line later cuts my hours, I'll apply to posted local food-plant jobs with safe duties and enough base pay for our remaining bills; I won't leave now for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background. The longer runway helps, but the thin bank balance is there this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay extra on the mortgage every month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check the loan statement first. Paying extra only works if food and school costs are covered and an extra paid shift is really there. I won't send the mortgage company money we need next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the order date, the number of paid seamer jobs and the actual posted base rates. If the supervisor has only a sales leaflet, I'd keep working and ask again in six months. A robot sales leaflet cannot feed a family.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes orders before capable robots reach seamers around 2039.
The shift should ask about **real jobs** before treating an unordered robot as certain.
think: At **56**, I may still owe on the mortgage and need wages.
The current **thin reserve** remains a problem even with ten years to prepare.
do: **Keep** working the seamer and check actual robot orders twice yearly.
**Pay** extra on mortgage from offered paid shifts after current bills.
**Apply** to posted safe local food jobs if hours cut and base pay enough.
feel: **Anxious** about current thin savings even with a longer runway.
S4.quote: A robot sales leaflet cannot feed a family.
fieldNote: He insists on **posted wages** and actual orders before treating a robot sales leaflet as a staffing decision.
Extra **mortgage payments** come only from newly earned offered shifts after current family costs.

steps.text: Keep running seamer while checking actual robot orders twice yearly
Pay extra mortgage principal from offered paid shifts after bills
Apply to posted safe local food jobs if hours cut and base pay enough

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut my seamer shifts while the children and mortgage still need them. Written notice, a real paid practical course if there is one, and posted safe local work with enough base pay would help. I need the hours on paper.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who opens a test tin after a robot runs the seamer. Soup on a shop shelf is a long way from our line, and a bad seam travels with it.

headlineQuote: Soup on a shop shelf is a long way from our line, and a bad seam travels with it.
portrait: **Carlos**, 43, is a mid-level soup-plant seamer operator with a vocational certificate and no AI use.
He and his office-cleaner partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with three weeks of expenses saved.
His **centre outlook** favors checking real rosters and posted wages over promises; he learns new controls only with paid practical instruction.
Fast robots make him **alarmed** about major hour loss, while his current low pay keeps him anxious even in quiet scenarios.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable seamer robots around 2031 and remove the hours that cover the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, offered paid practical training and posted safe local work with enough base pay would help.
